notes.title: Small tools. Long life.
notes.summary: A useful program should still make sense when you come back to it next year.
paragraphs: The tools I keep coming back to have a few things in common: a clear job, readable source, and a way to take my data with me. They do not need a subscription to remain useful.

That is the direction of this workshop. PHP for a small web interface, SQLite when a single file is enough, Python for a practical command-line task, and Go when a portable executable makes the job easier. The language follows the problem.
Simple does not mean careless. Validation, clear failure messages, a tested restore process, and useful documentation matter more than a complicated architecture.
CoolCode is where the runnable projects live. This site is the notebook beside the workbench: the questions, experiments, and decisions that connect them.

notes.title: A home for local DNS.
notes.summary: Local names and reverse lookups belong close to the machines they describe.
paragraphs: A home network becomes easier to understand when its services have names. A resolver can answer the questions about the local network and forward the rest to an upstream service.

The design I am exploring pairs dnsmasq for local records with an encrypted upstream resolver. The home.arpa namespace gives local names a clear boundary. Reverse lookups should be answered locally too.

The next useful layer is an inventory: when a device last appeared, which address it used, and what services it advertised. Discovery and publication should be separate steps, so an observed device does not automatically become a trusted DNS entry.
The goal is a network I can explain, export, and repair. A dashboard is useful only if the underlying records remain understandable.

notes.title: An archive is only useful if it opens.
notes.summary: Keeping the bytes is the beginning. Finding and reading them is the next job.
paragraphs: A directory of saved files is a good start. An archive becomes much more useful when it also preserves context: what a file is, where it came from, and how to open it.

Archive Shelf approaches the finding problem with full-text search and links back to original pages. Waystation approaches the disappearing-website problem with portable captures. Tape Index helps check whether the bytes still match a saved manifest.
These are different parts of the same habit: keep originals, make searchable derivatives, and keep enough information to reproduce the process.
I prefer an archive that remains usable without the software that created it. Plain text, conventional files, and documented exports make that a realistic goal.

ideas.title: Portfolio notebook
ideas.label: IBKR API / PERSONAL DASHBOARD
ideas.summary: A private place to understand positions, cash, and changes over time.
ideas.first_step: Start with a read-only view of one account’s positions, plus a local snapshot and a simple comparison against the previous snapshot.
ideas.questions: Choose the appropriate IBKR API and confirm account permissions, authentication, and data entitlements. Keep credentials server-side. The concept has no order-entry flow.

ideas.title: The long-way ride journal
ideas.label: STRAVA API / RIDES & EXPLORATION
ideas.summary: Connect rides with notes about the places, detours, and photographs worth remembering.
ideas.first_step: Prototype a private ride list for the connected athlete, with distance, date, and manually written field notes.
ideas.questions: Check Strava’s current access, subscription, display, and retention requirements before building. Keep exact routes and start/end locations private by default.

ideas.title: Small signals
ideas.label: ESP32 / MQTT / HOME LAB
ideas.summary: A small sensor project with a dashboard that makes its readings useful.
ideas.first_step: Try a low-voltage room sensor and a local MQTT topic. Save a simple history and display when the last reading arrived.
ideas.questions: Pick one useful measurement, decide how long to keep it, and show missing or stale data clearly. A desk display could be a later extension.

ideas.title: Contact sheet
ideas.label: PHOTOGRAPHY / PRIVATE ARCHIVES
ideas.summary: Find the photograph you remember by its light, mood, or subject.
ideas.first_step: Generate thumbnails from a small folder of copied images, add manual tags, and produce a portable contact sheet.
ideas.questions: Preserve originals and keep derivatives separate. Decide which metadata is useful privately and strip location data from public exports.

guides.title: Back up SQLite and check the copy
guides.summary: A small database deserves a real backup. Make a consistent snapshot, inspect it, and practise restoring away from production.
guides.needs: Linux shell, sqlite3 CLI, and read access to your existing database. Replace the example paths; keep backups outside the web root.

sections.heading: Start with a real database
sections.text: A typo in a database path can create an empty database. Open the source read-only and inspect its tables before you back it up. These examples use /srv/my-app/var/app.sqlite.
sections.check: Confirm you see the tables you expect, not an empty list.

sections.heading: Create a separate snapshot
sections.text: Make a private backup directory owned by your account. Use a new filename for each backup. The SQLite shell’s backup command takes a consistent database snapshot, including data that may currently be in a write-ahead log. Do not just copy the main file while an application is writing.
sections.check: Stop if the command reports an error. Keep the previous good backup.

sections.heading: Check, then rehearse recovery
sections.text: Open the copy, run an integrity check, and inspect the schema. An “ok” result checks database structure; it does not prove your application data is complete. Point a separate test copy of your application at the backup, with email, payments and background jobs disabled. Confirm expected records appear before you need a real recovery.
sections.check: Store another protected copy on a different device. A backup on the same disk cannot survive losing that disk.

guides.title: Test a new HTTPS server before changing DNS
guides.summary: Send one request to a new server while keeping the real hostname and normal certificate checks.
guides.needs: curl, a domain you manage, and the new server’s IP. Replace example.com and 192.0.2.10 (a documentation address).

sections.heading: Keep the hostname in the URL
sections.text: Using an IP address as the URL can select the wrong virtual host and certificate. A curl resolve override changes the destination for one hostname and port, while the URL keeps its hostname. The new server needs a valid certificate for that name.
sections.check: Look at the HTTP status and any Location header. This performs a GET and discards the response body.

sections.heading: Confirm where the request went
sections.text: Print the remote IP and status. --noproxy makes this a direct test; leave it out if your network requires an approved proxy, but understand that a proxy may resolve the destination instead.
sections.check: The reported IP should be the server you intended. Do not add -k to make a certificate failure disappear.

sections.heading: Check more than the homepage
sections.text: Repeat for a static asset and a representative application page. A redirect to www.example.com is a different hostname and needs its own override and certificate. Avoid automatically following redirects during this first check. This does not change DNS for anyone else; it also does not test browser JavaScript, logins or every application path.

guides.title: Why is Apache showing the wrong website?
guides.summary: Inspect the virtual-host map and configuration syntax before you restart anything.
guides.needs: An Apache 2.4 server you administer. Commands may need sudo to read configuration and certificate paths.

sections.heading: Ask Apache what it will load
sections.text: The command name varies by distribution. Debian and Ubuntu commonly use apache2ctl; other installations use apachectl. Run the matching pair, not both. These inspect the configuration on disk.
sections.check: Expected: Syntax OK, followed by a map of addresses, ports, hostnames and configuration-file locations.

sections.heading: Read the default and the names
sections.text: For each relevant address and port, compare ServerName and ServerAlias with the hostname you requested. Check which virtual host is the default for that address. A missing or mismatched name can send a request there. On systems with apachectl, the equivalent commands are:
sections.check: Check both port 80 and port 443. An HTTP redirect can be correct while the HTTPS virtual host is wrong.

sections.heading: Separate configuration from the running service
sections.text: The dump shows the configuration files now, which may differ from what the running process last loaded. Record the file and line number before editing. Verify DocumentRoot, the requested hostname and any reverse-proxy route. Re-run the syntax check after a change, then reload through your normal service-management procedure. A successful syntax check alone does not prove the site serves the intended content.

guides.title: Check an archive for changed files with SHA-256
guides.summary: Give a folder of photos, documents or exports a simple integrity record you can check later.
guides.needs: Linux with GNU find and sha256sum. A stable archive folder with no files being written during the scan.

sections.heading: Create the manifest outside the archive
sections.text: Work from the archive’s root so the stored paths remain relative. Use a fresh manifest filename; redirection overwrites an existing file. Keeping the manifest outside the scanned directory prevents it from hashing itself.
sections.check: Review any errors. This records regular files, not symlink targets, directory permissions or empty directories.

sections.heading: Verify from the same relative root
sections.text: After copying the archive to another disk, change into that copy and check against the saved manifest. Keep the folder layout the same.
sections.check: OK means a listed file matches. FAILED indicates changed bytes; a missing file produces an error. Newly added files are not detected by checking an older manifest.

sections.heading: Keep a trusted reference
sections.text: Checksums detect accidental changes only when you trust the manifest. Someone who can replace both the files and the manifest can make them match again. Keep a separate protected copy of the manifest. If a file fails, compare it with another backup before replacing anything. A checksum records integrity, not whether a photo is meaningful or a document can still be opened.

guides.title: Check local DNS in both directions
guides.summary: A device name can resolve correctly while reverse lookups still fail. Test each direction against the resolver you intended.
guides.needs: dig (BIND utilities), your local DNS server address, and a device with a known name and IP. Example addresses must be replaced.

sections.heading: Ask the local resolver directly
sections.text: Start with an explicit server so you know which resolver answers. Here, 192.168.1.2 is the example resolver and nas.home.arpa is the example device.
sections.check: An A record should contain the expected IPv4 address. Check the response status too; an empty answer is not automatically a timeout.

sections.heading: Look up the address in reverse
sections.text: Forward A records and reverse PTR records are separate. Creating one does not automatically create the other in every setup. Query the example device address.
sections.check: Look for a PTR record with the expected hostname. A trailing dot is normal in DNS output.

sections.heading: Compare with the client’s usual resolver
sections.text: Remove the explicit server to see how dig behaves using its resolver configuration. If the answers differ, inspect the client’s DNS settings before changing records. A browser using its own encrypted DNS may behave differently again.
sections.check: Use your local resolver for private names and addresses. home.arpa is intended for home networks; keep those records local rather than publishing them in public DNS.

guides.title: Run a small PHP site locally without a build step
guides.summary: A quick development loop for plain PHP: one public folder, one local server, and a clear boundary around private files.
guides.needs: PHP CLI and a project with public/index.php. Work from the project root; this example is for local development.

sections.heading: Check the CLI you are actually using
sections.text: The terminal PHP version can differ from the PHP used by Apache or PHP-FPM. Check the version and enabled modules before debugging an extension error.
sections.check: For PDO SQLite applications, look for PDO and pdo_sqlite. Your production PHP configuration must be checked separately.

sections.heading: Serve only the public directory
sections.text: Start from the project root. Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps this listener on loopback. The document root is public, so sibling config and database directories are outside the served tree.
sections.check: Open http://127.0.0.1:8080 in a browser on the same machine. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.

sections.heading: Add the application’s router when it has one
sections.text: For clean URLs, use the router supplied with the project. For this workshop repository the command is below. A router is PHP code, not an Apache .htaccess file. The built-in server is a development tool; use your normal Apache/PHP-FPM setup for public hosting.
sections.check: Keep secrets and database files out of public/. Check both a content page and a missing URL before calling the routing finished.

tips.title: Try the new server without changing DNS
tips.text: Use curl --resolve for a single hostname and port. Keep certificate verification enabled and check the actual remote IP.

tips.title: A database file copy is not always a backup
tips.text: For an active SQLite database, use a consistent snapshot. Then open and inspect the copy before trusting your backup routine.

tips.title: Ask Apache which site it thinks is first
tips.text: The virtual-host dump helps explain why an unexpected default site appears. Compare hostnames on both HTTP and HTTPS.

tips.title: Test names → addresses and addresses → names
tips.text: A successful forward lookup does not prove reverse DNS works. Check A and PTR records against the same local resolver.

tips.title: Keep the checksum manifest outside the scan
tips.text: A checksum file should not try to hash itself. Use relative paths so you can verify a restored copy on another disk.

tips.title: Make public/ the boundary
tips.text: Point the web server at the public directory. Keep application configuration, database files and backups beside it, outside the web root.
